title: Silicon in Plants: What It Does and When Palay Needs It
metaTitle: Silicon in Plants: Role in Rice, Signs and Sources
metaDescription: Silicon in plants stiffens rice leaves and stems against lodging, blast and planthoppers. See when palay needs it and why burning straw takes it away.
excerpt: Silicon in plants is not on the list of essential nutrients, yet palay takes more of it than of nitrogen. It stiffens the leaves and stems, so the crop stands up to wind, sheds blast and resists planthoppers and stem borers. Rice straw holds most of it, which is why burning or hauling away straw drains a field. Here is what it does and when palay needs it.

heroImage.alt: Ripe palay heads on stiff stems: silicon in plants keeps rice standing

blocks.text:
Rice lays silicon down as a thin glassy layer under the skin of its leaves, stems and husk. That layer stiffens the plant, holds the leaves upright toward the sun, slows water loss and makes the tissue harder for fungi and insects to get through.

So a palay crop with enough silicon lodges less, gets less blast and brown spot, and suffers less from planthoppers and stem borers. It also uses its nitrogen better, because upright leaves shade each other less.
A building block of the plant body

Silicon is a building block. Once laid down under the skin it stays there for good, and the straw carries most of it. A good palay crop can hold several hundred kilograms of silicon per hectare, more than its nitrogen.

It counts as a beneficial nutrient rather than an essential one, because rice can finish its life without it. In the field, though, a rice crop short of silicon is weaker in every way that matters to the yield.

blocks.caption: Silicon in short
rows: Droopy, soft leaves and more disease

blocks.text:
Silicon does not move once it is laid down, so new leaves rely on a steady supply. A rice crop short of it has soft, droopy leaves that bend over, more brown spot and blast, and stems that lodge easily.

See [silicon deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/silicon-deficiency) for the signs and fixes.
When silicon in plants is most critical

Palay needs silicon most from panicle initiation to heading, when it builds the stems that will carry the panicle and the leaves that will fill it, and it starts storing silicon from tillering. Sugarcane, mais and other grasses also take a lot of it.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing silicon in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

blocks.text: What keeps silicon from the crop

Old, heavily weathered soils, sandy soils and peat hold little silicon the roots can take. Fields cropped twice a year for many years, with the straw burned or carried away, run down fastest.

Returning the straw puts most of the silicon back. That is one of the best reasons to work straw into the field instead of burning it.

Rice straw and rice hull ash are the cheapest silicon, and they cost nothing if they come from your own field. Calcium silicate slags and potassium silicate sprays are also sold. See [balanced fertilization for rice](/blog/balanced-fertilization-for-rice).

items: Rice straw worked back into the field: most of the silicon the crop took.
Rice hull ash and carbonized rice hull: silicon and some potassium.
Calcium silicate: on the soil, also raises the pH a little.
Potassium silicate: a spray, with potassium too.

blocks.title: Silicon does not replace good nitrogen and potassium
blocks.text: Silicon makes a crop stand better and resist pests, but it cannot fix a field short of nitrogen or potassium. Use it alongside a balanced program, not instead of one.

items.q: Is silicon a nutrient for rice?
items.a: Silicon is a beneficial nutrient. Rice can live without it, but it takes more silicon than nitrogen and grows much stronger with it.
It helps a lot. Silicon stiffens the stems and leaves, so the crop stands better in wind and rain.

items.q: Why should I not burn rice straw?
items.a: Burning sends the straw's sulfur and nitrogen up in smoke and leaves its silicon and potassium in ash that blows or washes away. Working the straw in returns them to the soil.

items.q: When should I apply silicon to palay?
items.a: Before or early in tillering on the soil, or as sprays from active tillering to heading.
